newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin returns to Kremlin, foes plot his removal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin returns to Kremlin, foes plot his removal.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, anxious to prove he is well enough to rule Russia, returned unexpectedly to the Kremlin on Wednesday as parliament debated a proposal to try to dismiss him because of ill-health.
Yeltsin arrived in his office just two days after leaving hospital following 12 days of treatment for double pneumonia and going to an official residence outside Moscow to convalesce.
Apparently defying doctors' recommendations not to rush his return to work, Yeltsin went to the Kremlin for talks with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
"President Yeltsin arrived at the Kremlin at 11.30 this morning (0830 GMT)," a Kremlin spokesman said.
The 65-year-old president is clearly worried that his illness, so soon after heart surgery in November, could play into his rivals' hands.
Shortly after he arrived in the Kremlin, the State Duma lower house of parliament started to debate a motion to dismiss him because of his poor health.

Yeltsin spent six months out of the Kremlin last year with heart problems and had been back at his office for only two weeks before catching pneumonia. His rivals say he is not up to running this vast country of 150 million people.
"Either we agree to Russia's collapse or try to do something about it," communist Viktor Ilyukhin, who initiated the resolution demanding his removal, told reporters.
Itar-Tass news agency said the chamber was likely to vote on the motion at about six p.m. (1500 GMT).

Yeltsin's parliamentary representative, Alexander Kotenkov, told deputies they could face a tough response if they passed the resolution, which he said would have no legal force but could have dangerous implications.
"The phrase "The President is dismissed' may be taken by some members of society as an excuse not to carry out presidential orders," he said, referring to the wording of the resolution.
Kotenkov did not say what measures the Kremlin had in mind.

"There is a legal term "the prevention of greater harm'. When discussing this draft I call on you to imagine what measures might be taken by other branches of power to prevent a greater harm," he said.
Parliament's own legal department has already said the motion, launched after Yeltsin was taken to hospital with pneumonia on January 8, cannot be used to oust the president.

Nikolai Ryzhkov, a former Soviet prime minister and an ally of the communists, said the motion violated the constitution and the Duma should instead prepare laws to clarify procdures for removing a president because of ill health.
The pro-government "Our Home is Russia" group and the liberal opposition "Yabloko" party walked out of the chamber at the beginning of the debate.
"I call on you not to take part in this humiliating show," said "Our Home" leader Sergei Belyaev before the walkout.
Yabloko leader Grigory Yavlinsky then reappeared and told the Duma that the motion had little to do with changing policy.
"It is a provocation," he said of the move, backed by communist and nationalist parliamentary groups.

Yavlinsky said these factions were now trying to distance themselves from Yeltsin and attempting to prove they were in opposition after earlier backing the government's draft budget for 1997, "a budget which robbed the country..."
The Kremlin's chief doctor said on Tuesday that Yeltsin, who has not been seen in public since he came down with pneumonia, was perfectly capable of ruling the country.
But opposition politicians blame Yeltsin's absence for a host of problems dogging Russia, including long delays in state pension and wage payments.
The Kremlin spokesman said these issues were discussed by Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin at their talks, as well as elections next week in rebel Chechnya.
